claims.text: Elevated-temperature aging in the presence of trace oxygen or nitrogen promotes phase segregation or second-phase formation in a nominally single-phase high-entropy alloy.
Local compositional fluctuations independently cause partial transformation of the nominal single-phase structure.
Second phases or segregated regions weaken dislocation- and twin-mediated toughening.
The impurity-associated microstructural transformation promotes embrittlement and brittle fracture.
The initial material is a compositionally uniform, single-phase FCC or BCC high-entropy alloy without visible second-phase precipitates.
The initial single-phase material has high ductility and toughness at ambient conditions.
Increasing oxygen or nitrogen to 0.5–2 at% and aging for up to tens of hours will accelerate segregation or precipitation.
The controlled comparison uses nanopillar compression or micro-tensile testing at 700–800 °C on low-impurity, short-annealed specimens versus impurity-enriched or extended-aged specimens.
Second-phase precipitates and impurity-segregated zones disrupt dislocation slip near the crack front.
Second-phase precipitates and impurity-segregated zones disrupt twin-boundary interactions near the crack front.
Twin-mediated crack-tip bridging can impede fracture in a single-phase high-entropy alloy.
Emergent precipitates and impurity-rich zones locally pin dislocations.
Dislocation pinning and reduced twin-mediated toughening promote microcrack formation at stress concentrators.
Impurity-enriched or aged samples will have lower fracture toughness than the as-processed single-phase baseline.
Impurity-enriched or aged samples will initiate cracks earlier than the as-processed baseline.
The predicted toughness loss and earlier crack initiation will correlate with observable segregation or second-phase formation.
The proposed embrittlement regime is sustained service at 700–800 °C with oxygen or nitrogen above 0.5 at% for sufficient time to permit segregation or precipitation.
Localized ordering or other microstructural instabilities could also contribute to embrittlement.
The experiment tracks crack initiation, strain localization, second-phase or segregation evolution, dislocation configurations, and twin-boundary activity under matched loading.
Finding neither second-phase development nor a change in crack initiation or growth after impurity enrichment or high-temperature exposure would falsify the proposed impurity-driven mechanism.
